era: The First Arrow Shot for Islam
teaser: 'Shoot, Sa'd — may my father and mother be your ransom.' The Prophet ﷺ said that of no one else.

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: The Prophet ﷺ called him 'my uncle'
layers.content:
Sa'd ibn Malik ibn Wuhayb ibn Abd Manaf ibn Zuhra ibn Kilab — Abu Waqqas was his father's byname, and Malik his name. Sa'd's kunya was Abu Ishaq and his mother was Hamna bint Sufyan ibn Umayya. Banu Zuhra was the clan of Aminah bint Wahb, the Prophet's ﷺ mother, and the Prophet ﷺ acknowledged the tie openly. Jabir ibn Abdullah saw Sa'd arrive while the Prophet ﷺ was sitting, and the Prophet ﷺ said: this is my uncle, so let a man honour his uncle.

Sa'd once asked him directly, 'Messenger of Allah, who am I?' The answer was his full lineage, ending: and if anyone says otherwise, the curse of Allah is on him. He had asked to be told where he stood, and was given a line he could not be argued out of.

His daughter Aisha bint Sa'd described him as short and stout and rough-built, with a large head, thick fingers and a great deal of hair. He dyed it black. In old age he was seen leading the prayer in a fur coat, and he glorified Allah counting on pebbles. He wore a gold ring, and if he wanted to eat garlic, he ate garlic.
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ of Sa'd: 'This is my uncle, so esteem his uncle' — reported from Jabir ibn Abdullah, Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: Seventeen, and one third of the religion
layers.content:
He put his own position in the plainest possible terms: no man became Muslim before me except one man who became Muslim on the same day. And then the sentence that fixes the picture — 'I remember when I was a third of Islam.'

A third. Three people. His daughter Aisha bint Sa'd heard him say he was seventeen years old. Another of his remarks dates it more sharply still: on the day I became Muslim, Allah had not yet prescribed the prayers.

So his entry into Islam predates almost everything a Muslim today would recognise as Islam. There was no prayer to perform, no qiblah, no fast, no community. There was a man saying that Allah is one and that he had been sent, and a seventeen-year-old of Banu Zuhra deciding that this was true and worth his life.

What he chose cost him early. He speaks of an expedition where the Muslims had nothing to eat but the leaves of thorn trees and acacia, and describes the state it reduced them to without softening it. Then, he says, Banu Asad came at him over the religion — and the fear he names is not for his body but that his deeds might be lost.
layers.source: Reported from Amir ibn Sa'd and Aisha bint Sa'd — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: The archer, and the brother he armed
layers.content:
'By Allah, I was the first man of the Arabs to shoot an arrow in the way of Allah.' He said it about the expedition of Ubayda ibn al-Harith, sixty riders, in the earliest days of armed defence. Al-Qasim ibn Abd ar-Rahman states it flatly too: Sa'd ibn Malik was the first to shoot an arrow in the cause of Allah.

At Badr he was so young that, in his own words, there was not a hair on his face. Before the army left he found his younger brother Umayr hiding, and asked why. 'I am afraid the Messenger of Allah ﷺ will see me and think me too young and send me back — and I want to go out so Allah might grant me martyrdom.' The Prophet ﷺ did tell him to go back. Umayr wept, and was allowed. Sa'd tied the sword-belt on him himself, because the boy was too small to manage it. Umayr was killed at Badr at sixteen.

At Uhud the Prophet ﷺ called out to Sa'd: shoot, Sa'd — may my father and mother be your ransom. Ali ibn Abi Talib said he never heard the Prophet ﷺ offer both his parents in ransom for anyone else.
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ at Uhud: 'Shoot, Sa'd. May my father and mother be your ransom' — reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: The archer who put the bow down
layers.content:
The man who fired Islam's first arrow, who commanded the armies that took al-Mada'in, refused to shoot when Muslims turned on each other.

Asked what kept him from the fighting, he said: not until they bring me a sword that knows a believer from an unbeliever. He said it more than once, and more fully: I do not claim this shirt of mine has any better right to the caliphate. I struggled when I knew what struggle was, and I did not throw my life away while there was a man better than me. I will not fight until they bring me a sword with two eyes, a tongue and two lips, that says, this one is a believer and this one is an unbeliever.

The same carefulness governed his speech. As-Sa'ib ibn Yazid travelled with him from Madinah to Makkah and back and did not hear him narrate a single hadith the whole way. Asked about a matter once, he answered under his breath, and explained: I am afraid of telling you one thing and having you add a hundred to it.

He had fought where fighting was clear and stopped where it was not. That is a harder discipline than courage.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: The illness that gave the ummah its bequest rule
layers.content:
He fell dangerously ill in Makkah and the Prophet ﷺ came to visit him. Sa'd was afraid of dying in the city he had emigrated out of. The Prophet ﷺ said three times: O Allah, heal Sa'd.

Then Sa'd asked about his money. He had a great deal and, at that point, one daughter to inherit it. Shall I will away all of it? No. Two-thirds? No. Half? No. A third? 'A third — and a third is a lot. It is better to leave your heirs wealthy than to leave them begging from people. Whatever you spend on your family is sadaqah, even the morsel you lift to your wife's mouth.' That exchange is where the one-third limit on bequests comes from. The Prophet ﷺ added: perhaps Allah will let you live, and some people will be benefited through you and others harmed.

He lived roughly another forty years, and Umar sent him to command in Iraq. He died at his estate in al-Aqiq, about ten miles from Madinah, in 55 AH, aged around seventy — reports differ, and one gives 50 AH. Men carried his bier in on their shoulders, and the wives of the Prophet ﷺ had it brought into the mosque so they could pray over him.
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ on bequests: 'A third, and a third is a lot. It is better that you leave your children wealthy than to leave them needy, having to importune people' — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III; the report is also in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Book of Wills
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

quiz.prompt: How did Sa'd describe his own place among the earliest Muslims?

options.text: 'I was the fortieth to enter'
'I remember when I was a third of Islam'
'I was the first of Banu Zuhra'
'I entered on the day of the house of al-Arqam'

quiz.citation: Reported from Amir ibn Sa'd from his father — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was seventeen, and on the day he became Muslim the prayers had not yet been prescribed. He committed to the religion before the religion had its shape.

quiz.prompt: What did Sa'd claim to be the first man of the Arabs to do?

options.text: Give the adhan
Ride out on horseback at Badr
Shoot an arrow in the way of Allah
Emigrate to Madinah

quiz.citation: Reported from Qays ibn Abi Hazim and from al-Qasim ibn Abd ar-Rahman — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He tied the claim to the expedition of Ubayda ibn al-Harith, sixty riders. In the same breath he describes eating thorn-tree leaves — the first arrow was fired by a hungry man.

quiz.prompt: Why was Sa'd's younger brother Umayr hiding before the army left for Badr?

options.text: He had no weapon of his own
He was afraid the Prophet ﷺ would judge him too young and send him back
He had not told their mother he was going
He was afraid of the fighting

quiz.citation: Reported from Amir ibn Sa'd from his father — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was sent back, wept, and was allowed. Sa'd had to buckle the sword-belt on him because he was too small to do it himself. He was killed at Badr at sixteen.

quiz.prompt: What did Sa'd say he was waiting for before he would fight in the conflicts between Muslims?

options.text: A ruling from the surviving Companions
Permission from Aisha
A sword with eyes, a tongue and lips, that could say which man was a believer
The return of his sons from Iraq

quiz.citation: Reported from Muhammad ibn Sirin and from Yahya ibn al-Husayn — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He said in the same breath that he did not consider himself entitled to the caliphate, and that he had never thrown his life away while a better man than him was there. Restraint, not confusion.

quiz.prompt: When Sa'd asked how much of his wealth he could will away, what did the Prophet ﷺ permit?

options.text: All of it, since he had only one daughter
Two-thirds
Half
A third — and even that, he said, is a lot

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III; the report is also in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Book of Wills
quiz.scholar_reflection: The one-third ceiling on bequests in Islamic law comes from this bedside conversation. The reason given was not stinginess but the dignity of his heirs: better wealthy than begging.

quiz.prompt: Sa'd asked the Prophet ﷺ outright, 'Who am I?' — and was given his lineage. Where do you go when you need to be told who you are?

options.text: Family and where I come from
What I have built or done
What Allah has said about people like me
I have not found a place that answers it

quiz.citation: Reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The answer he got was not a compliment. It was a fact, given with a warning against anyone who would dispute it. Some reassurance works precisely because it is not flattering.

quiz.prompt: Umayr hid so no one would stop him going to a battle he might not survive. What do you hide because someone would talk you out of it?
quiz.slider_label: What you keep out of sight

options.text: Ambitions people would call unrealistic
Acts of worship I do not want discussed
Costs I have decided to accept alone
Nothing — I say everything out loud

quiz.citation: Reflection on the account of Umayr ibn Abi Waqqas — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: His brother found him out and did not stop him. He tied the boy's sword on instead. Not every love protects by preventing.

quiz.prompt: Sa'd, an expert archer, refused to shoot when he could not tell right from wrong. When you cannot see clearly, what do you do?

options.text: Act anyway — inaction is also a choice
Wait, and accept being called a coward for it
Follow whoever I trust most
Look for the smallest safe step and take that

quiz.citation: Reflection on Sa'd's refusal to fight in the fitnah — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: His answer was concrete rather than pious: bring me a sword that can tell. He wanted certainty of a kind that does not exist, and he was honest that he did not have it.

quiz.prompt: He barely narrated hadith, afraid one word of his would become a hundred in someone else's mouth. What do you do with the risk of being misquoted?

options.text: Say less, and only what I am sure of
Say it clearly and let people carry it as they will
Add so many qualifications that the point gets lost
I have not thought about it much

quiz.citation: Reported from as-Sa'ib ibn Yazid — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: A companion travelled with him from Madinah to Makkah and back and heard him narrate nothing. The silence of someone with that much to say is itself information.

quiz.prompt: 'Better to leave your heirs wealthy than begging' — the Prophet ﷺ capped his charity for his family's sake. How do you balance giving with providing?

options.text: My family comes first and I do not apologise for it
I give generously and worry whether it is fair to them
I under-give in both directions and call it prudence
I have never had to make the trade-off

quiz.citation: Reflection on the Prophet's ﷺ instruction to Sa'd — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Notice the widening in the same hadith: the morsel you raise to your wife's mouth counts as sadaqah. Providing was not set against charity; it was named as a form of it.
